questions.stem:
You are about to leave school after spending six years as a student. Write a letter to the principal, expressing your candid views on the strengths and weaknesses of the school and giving suggestions for improvement.

(Your answer should not be less than 400 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — candid, balanced views: at least two strengths (e.g. discipline, good results, sports) and two weaknesses (e.g. inadequate laboratory/library, poor hostel facilities) with practical suggestions for improvement; respectful tone
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, inside address, salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), a suitable heading, well-paragraphed body with introduction and conclusion, and formal subscription (Yours faithfully, signature and full name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A formal letter to the Principal headed e.g. 'MY VIEWS ON THE SCHOOL AS I LEAVE'. The writer thanks the principal for six years of training, then praises strengths such as discipline, dedicated teachers and good examination results; respectfully points out weaknesses such as an ill-equipped library and laboratories, overcrowded hostels and poor water supply; and suggests remedies such as PTA/old-students' fund-raising, regular maintenance and more prefect involvement. It closes with good wishes and 'Yours faithfully', signature and full name.

questions.stem:
Write an article for publication in a literary magazine on the need to promote the study of the indigenous languages of your country.

(Your answer should not be less than 400 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — reasons for promoting indigenous languages (preservation of culture and identity, better early learning in the mother tongue, national unity, literature and oral tradition) and ways of promoting them (school curricula, media, literary prizes, government policy)
10 marks: Organisation: suitable title, writer's name (and status/address where required), engaging introduction, logically developed paragraphs and a firm conclusion
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: Title e.g. 'Saving Our Mother Tongues', with the writer's name. The article notes that many young people can no longer speak their mother tongue, then argues that indigenous languages carry the people's culture, proverbs and history; that children learn better in the mother tongue; and that they foster pride and identity. It recommends compulsory study in schools, more books, radio and television programmes in the languages, literary competitions and government support, and concludes that a people who lose their language lose themselves.

questions.stem:
You are the main speaker in a school debate the topic of which is: Bribery and corruption are worse enemies of our country than armed robbery.
Write your speech for or against the topic.

(Your answer should not be less than 400 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — a clear stand for or against the motion supported by convincing points, e.g. (for) corruption affects the whole nation, diverts public funds, destroys institutions and even breeds armed robbery; (against) armed robbery takes lives directly and creates fear and insecurity
10 marks: Organisation: vocatives (e.g. The Chairman, Principal, panel of judges, co-debaters), self-introduction and statement of the motion/stand, logically developed points in paragraphs, a strong conclusion and appreciation (e.g. Thank you for listening)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: Begins 'Mr Chairman, panel of judges, ... I am here to support the motion...'. Points (for): bribery and corruption steal funds meant for roads, hospitals and schools, affecting millions; they corrupt the police and courts so that even armed robbers go free; they discourage investment and cause unemployment, which in turn breeds robbery; their effects are long-lasting while a robbery affects a few people. The speaker rebuts the opposition and concludes by urging the audience to vote for the motion, thanking them for listening.

questions.stem:
You have been involved in an incident in which very many of your friends criticized your role. Narrate the incident to a close friend and defend the role you played.

(Your answer should not be less than 400 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — a clear narration of a credible incident, the criticism received, and a convincing defence/justification of the role played; written as a letter to a close friend
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, informal salutation (e.g. Dear Ada), introductory paragraph, well-linked paragraphs, conclusion and informal subscription (e.g. Yours sincerely/Your loving brother, first name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: An informal letter: after greetings, the writer narrates e.g. how he reported classmates who planned to steal examination questions or how she refused to join a protest that turned violent. Friends called him a traitor/coward. He defends his role: he acted to protect the school's integrity and his friends' future, avoided greater punishment for all, and followed his conscience. He asks for his friend's understanding and closes warmly.

questions.stem:
An elder sister of yours who has left school had confided to you in her last letter that she plans to elope with her lover whom your parents do not approve of. Write a letter to her advising her against such an action, and suggesting steps she could take to obtain your parents' consent.

(Your answer should not be less than 400 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — reasons against eloping (disgrace to the family, loss of parental blessing and support, insecurity if the relationship fails) and practical steps to win consent (patience, introducing the man properly, involving respected relatives/elders or the pastor/imam, the man showing responsibility)
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, informal salutation (e.g. Dear Ada), introductory paragraph, well-linked paragraphs, conclusion and informal subscription (e.g. Yours sincerely/Your loving brother, first name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: An informal letter opening 'Dear Sister'. The writer acknowledges her letter and feelings, then warns that eloping would disgrace the family, cut her off from parental blessing and support, and leave her with nobody to turn to if things go wrong. She suggests that the suitor formally visit the parents, that respected uncles/aunts or the family pastor intercede, that she give the parents time and show the man's good qualities, and promises her own help. She closes with love.

questions.stem:
Write a story which ends with the words: ... I really agree that a patient dog eats the fattest bone.

(Your answer should not be less than 400 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — an interesting, original story in which patience is eventually rewarded (e.g. a character who waits or endures while others rush and fail) and which ends exactly with the given words
10 marks: Organisation: an arresting opening, a coherent plot with events in logical sequence, a climax, and an ending that leads naturally to the given words
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A story such as: two friends finish school; one rushes into a dubious get-rich-quick scheme and loses everything, while the narrator patiently learns a trade/waits for admission, working hard through hardship. Years later the narrator succeeds — a scholarship or thriving business — while the impatient friend regrets his haste. The narrator reflects on events and ends: '... I really agree that a patient dog eats the fattest bone.'

questions.stem:
Your family has recently moved to a new environment. Write a letter to your best friend describing the environment and stating what you dislike about the place.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — vivid description of the new environment (location, houses, roads, people, amenities) and clear statement of at least two or three dislikes (e.g. noise, dirt, flooding, insecurity, poor water/electricity)
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, informal salutation (e.g. Dear Ada), introductory paragraph, well-linked paragraphs, conclusion and informal subscription (e.g. Yours sincerely/Your loving brother, first name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: An informal letter: after greetings, the writer explains that the family has moved (e.g. to a new estate on the outskirts of the city), describes the streets, houses, market, neighbours and school, and then states dislikes such as refuse heaps and blocked gutters, loud music from a nearby beer parlour, erratic electricity and the long distance to school. The writer says he/she misses the friend, invites him/her to visit, and closes warmly.

questions.stem:
Write an article for publication in one of your national newspapers discussing ways of improving the standard of education in your country.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — relevant, well-developed ways of improving education: adequate funding, well-trained and well-paid teachers, provision of facilities (libraries, laboratories), regular supervision/inspection, curbing examination malpractice, involving parents and communities, reviewing curricula
10 marks: Organisation: suitable title, writer's name (and status/address where required), engaging introduction, logically developed paragraphs and a firm conclusion
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: Title e.g. 'Raising the Standard of Education', with the writer's name. The article notes falling standards (mass failure, malpractice), then discusses remedies: increased government funding; recruitment, training and prompt payment of teachers; provision of books, laboratories and libraries; effective inspection; severe sanctions against examination malpractice; parental involvement; and a relevant curriculum. It concludes that education is the bedrock of development.

questions.stem:
There has been a wave of killings in your locality. Write a letter to the Editor of one of your national newspapers condemning this evil act and suggesting at least three ways of curbing it.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — condemnation of the killings with brief description of their effects (fear, loss of lives, flight of residents) and at least three practical ways of curbing them (more police patrols, community vigilance groups, street lighting, prosecution of offenders, employment for youths)
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, inside address, salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), a suitable heading, well-paragraphed body with introduction and conclusion, and formal subscription (Yours faithfully, signature and full name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A formal letter to 'The Editor' with a heading such as 'END THE KILLINGS IN OUR COMMUNITY'. The writer describes the spate of killings, condemns them as barbaric, and states their effects. He suggests increased police presence and patrols, formation of vigilance groups that cooperate with the police, provision of streetlights, quick prosecution of culprits, and job creation for idle youths. Ends 'Yours faithfully', signature and name.

questions.stem:
You have been chosen to speak to the youths in your town on the dangers of bush-burning. Write out the speech you would deliver on the occasion.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — the dangers of bush-burning: destruction of vegetation, wildlife and farms/crops, loss of soil fertility and erosion, destruction of property and lives, air pollution and contribution to desertification; with appeal/suggestions for prevention
10 marks: Organisation: vocatives (e.g. The Chairman, Principal, panel of judges, co-debaters), self-introduction and statement of the motion/stand, logically developed points in paragraphs, a strong conclusion and appreciation (e.g. Thank you for listening)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: Opens with vocatives (the Chairman, community leaders, fellow youths). The speaker explains why some people burn bush (hunting, clearing farms) and then the dangers: it destroys plants and animals, exposes the soil to erosion and kills soil organisms, spreads to farms and houses, pollutes the air and encourages desert encroachment. He urges youths to stop the practice, to create fire breaks, and to report offenders, then thanks the audience.

questions.stem:
Write a story, real or imagined, which illustrates the saying: "Don't count your chickens before they are hatched."

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — an interesting story in which a character confidently counts on an expected gain or outcome which fails to materialise, clearly illustrating the saying
10 marks: Organisation: an arresting opening, a coherent plot with events in logical sequence, a climax, and an ending that leads naturally to the given words
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A story: a student expecting a car from his rich uncle after his examination boasts to everyone and even sells his old bicycle; he neglects his studies, sure of success. The uncle's business collapses, no car comes, and he also fails some subjects. He learns, bitterly, not to count his chickens before they are hatched.

questions.stem:
You have recently moved into a new neighbourhood with your parents. Write a letter to your sister who is studying overseas giving, at least, three reasons for disliking the new place.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — a brief description of the new neighbourhood and at least three clear, well-developed reasons for disliking it (e.g. insecurity, noise, poor sanitation, flooding, lack of water/electricity, unfriendly neighbours)
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, informal salutation (e.g. Dear Ada), introductory paragraph, well-linked paragraphs, conclusion and informal subscription (e.g. Yours sincerely/Your loving brother, first name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: An informal letter to 'Dear Sister' with the writer's (home) address and date. After asking about her studies abroad, the writer explains that the family has moved and describes the area briefly. Reasons for disliking it: frequent burglaries and insecurity at night; deafening noise from a nearby motor park and churches; heaps of refuse and flooded streets whenever it rains; and irregular power and water supply. The writer hopes the family will move again, sends greetings from parents and closes 'Your loving brother/sister' with first name.

questions.stem:
Write an article for publication in a national newspaper on the topic: Vocational Training is the answer to unemployment among the youths.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — arguments showing how vocational training reduces youth unemployment: self-employment and entrepreneurship, practical skills employers need, reduced dependence on white-collar jobs, job creation for others, reduction of crime; plus suggestions (skill centres, funding, loans, changing attitudes)
10 marks: Organisation: suitable title, writer's name (and status/address where required), engaging introduction, logically developed paragraphs and a firm conclusion
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: Title, e.g. 'Vocational Training: The Answer to Youth Unemployment', and the writer's name. The article describes the large number of jobless graduates, then argues that skills such as tailoring, welding, ICT, catering and electrical installation enable youths to be self-employed, to employ others, and to meet industry's demand for technicians; it reduces crime and restiveness. It urges government to build and equip vocational centres, give soft loans and change the attitude that only white-collar jobs are respectable, and concludes that vocational training is the surest path to self-reliance.

questions.stem:
Your country's Public Transport System is not functioning properly. Write a letter to the Minister of Transport highlighting the causes and suggesting, at least, two measures to remedy the situation.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — causes of the poor public transport system (bad roads, inadequate and old vehicles, poor funding and maintenance, corruption/mismanagement, neglect of rail and water transport) and at least two practical remedies (road repairs, more buses, revival of railways, proper management, regulation)
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, inside address, salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), a suitable heading, well-paragraphed body with introduction and conclusion, and formal subscription (Yours faithfully, signature and full name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A formal letter to 'The Honourable Minister of Transport', with heading e.g. 'THE POOR STATE OF PUBLIC TRANSPORT'. Causes: dilapidated roads, too few and old buses, neglect of the railways, poor maintenance culture, mismanagement and corruption, and indiscipline among drivers. Remedies: repair and expand roads, buy more mass-transit buses, revive the railways and inland waterways, train drivers and enforce traffic rules, and hand some services to efficient private operators. Ends 'Yours faithfully', signature and full name.

questions.stem:
You are the Chief Speaker in a debate on the topic: The youths of today are more interested in the pursuit of pleasure than in academic work.
Write your speech for or against the topic.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — a clear stand with convincing points, e.g. (for) addiction to social media, parties, films, football betting, fashion; poor reading culture; examination malpractice; (against) many youths win academic competitions and scholarships, crowd libraries and tutorials, pursue higher degrees
10 marks: Organisation: vocatives (e.g. The Chairman, Principal, panel of judges, co-debaters), self-introduction and statement of the motion/stand, logically developed points in paragraphs, a strong conclusion and appreciation (e.g. Thank you for listening)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: Begins 'Mr Chairman, panel of judges, accurate time-keeper, co-debaters... I am here to support the motion'. Points: youths spend hours on phones, chatting and watching films; parties and clubbing fill weekends; football viewing centres and betting shops are full of students while libraries are empty; examination malpractice shows they want success without study; poor results in public examinations confirm it. The speaker rebuts the opposition's examples as exceptions, urges the audience to vote for the motion, and thanks them.

questions.stem:
Write a story to illustrate the saying: A good name is better than riches.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — an interesting story in which a character's reputation/integrity proves more valuable than money (e.g. an honest person is trusted, helped or rewarded while a rich but dishonest person is disgraced), clearly illustrating the saying
10 marks: Organisation: an arresting opening, a coherent plot with events in logical sequence, a climax, and an ending that leads naturally to the given words
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A story: a poor but honest trader, Ade, returns a bag of money a stranger forgot in his shop; the stranger turns out to be a wealthy businessman who later gives him a contract. Meanwhile a rich neighbour known for cheating is arrested and abandoned by friends. When Ade's shop burns down, the whole community contributes to rebuild it because of his good name. The narrator concludes that a good name is better than riches.

questions.stem:
A friend of yours confided in you that she intends to drop out of school to get married. Write a letter to her giving, at least, three reasons why she should stay in school.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — at least three convincing reasons for staying in school (education gives a secure future and financial independence; early marriage carries health risks and limits opportunities; an educated mother raises better children; marriage can wait while the right man will wait too), with a persuasive, friendly tone
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, informal salutation (e.g. Dear Ada), introductory paragraph, well-linked paragraphs, conclusion and informal subscription (e.g. Yours sincerely/Your loving brother, first name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: An informal letter opening 'Dear Ngozi'. The writer acknowledges her confidence and expresses concern, then argues: education will make her financially independent rather than wholly dependent on a husband; early marriage and childbirth endanger a young girl's health; an educated woman is better able to raise and teach her children; she may regret abandoning her dreams; a suitor who truly loves her will wait. The writer urges her to discuss with her parents and teachers, promises support, and closes 'Your friend', first name.

questions.stem:
Write an article suitable for publication in a national newspaper on the menace of indecent dressing in the society.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — the meaning and forms of indecent dressing, its causes (foreign films/media influence, peer pressure, poor parental guidance, fashion industry) and effects (moral decadence, sexual harassment, disrespect, poor image), with remedies (parental guidance, school dress codes, religious/moral teaching, media regulation)
10 marks: Organisation: suitable title, writer's name (and status/address where required), engaging introduction, logically developed paragraphs and a firm conclusion
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: Title, e.g. 'Indecent Dressing: A Threat to Our Values', with the writer's name. The writer describes revealing and sagging clothes seen on streets and campuses, traces the causes to foreign films, music videos, social media and peer pressure, and shows the effects: erosion of cultural values, provocation of harassment and rape, and loss of respect. Remedies: parents and teachers as role models, enforced dress codes in schools and offices, religious and moral instruction, and media censorship. Concludes with a call to restore decency.

questions.stem:
Your school has been performing poorly in public examinations for the past three years. Write a letter to your principal suggesting ways of making the students more interested in academic work.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — practical suggestions to arouse students' interest in academic work: reward/prizes for excellence, well-stocked library and laboratories, more qualified/motivated teachers, academic clubs and competitions, supervised prep/study periods, guidance and counselling, involving parents, discouraging malpractice and distractions
10 marks: Organisation: writer's address and date, inside address, salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), a suitable heading, well-paragraphed body with introduction and conclusion, and formal subscription (Yours faithfully, signature and full name)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A formal letter to the Principal headed 'WAYS OF IMPROVING STUDENTS' INTEREST IN ACADEMIC WORK'. The writer notes the poor results of the past three years, then suggests: prizes and scholarships for outstanding students; equipping the library and laboratories; organising quiz, debate and science clubs; supervised evening prep; regular tests with feedback; motivational talks by successful old students; counselling; and close cooperation with parents through the PTA. Ends 'Yours faithfully', signature and name.

questions.stem:
You are the chief speaker in a debate on the topic: "Religious education should be made compulsory in schools." Write your argument for or against the topic.

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — a clear stand with well-developed points, e.g. (for) instils moral values and discipline, reduces vices such as cultism and exam malpractice, promotes tolerance and good citizenship; (against) religion is a private/family matter, compulsion breeds conflict in a multi-religious society, crowds the timetable, morals can be taught through civic education
10 marks: Organisation: vocatives (e.g. The Chairman, Principal, panel of judges, co-debaters), self-introduction and statement of the motion/stand, logically developed points in paragraphs, a strong conclusion and appreciation (e.g. Thank you for listening)
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: Opens with vocatives and the speaker's stand (e.g. for the motion). Arguments: moral decline among youths (cultism, drug abuse, examination malpractice) calls for religious education; it teaches honesty, respect and the fear of God; it promotes tolerance when students learn about religion; it complements civic education in producing good citizens. The speaker rebuts the claim that religion is private and closes by urging support for the motion, thanking the audience.

questions.stem:
Write a story that illustrates the saying: "You reap what you sow."

(Your answer should not be less than 450 words.)
questions.markingGuide:
10 marks: Content — an interesting story in which a character's actions (good or bad) clearly bring corresponding consequences, illustrating the saying
10 marks: Organisation: an arresting opening, a coherent plot with events in logical sequence, a climax, and an ending that leads naturally to the given words
20 marks: Expression — appropriate vocabulary and register, varied and correct sentence structures, effective paragraphing and good flow of ideas
10 marks: Mechanical accuracy — correct grammar, spelling and punctuation (marks deducted for each type of error)
questions.explanation: A story: Tunde, a lazy and dishonest student, bullies others and relies on cheating; he is caught in the final examination, his results are cancelled and he becomes a labourer. His diligent classmate Musa, whom he mocked, studies hard, gains admission and later becomes a doctor — the doctor who eventually treats Tunde after an accident. Tunde reflects that we reap what we sow.

questions.explanation: Frugal (careful with money) is the opposite of extravagant (wasteful).

Poor feeding has caused children of this village to suffer from ..........
questions.explanation: Malnutrition results from poor feeding.

questions.stem:

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

Our instructor gave us the impression that the problem was [complicated] but we found it ..........
questions.explanation: The opposite of complicated is simple.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

It is no longer a matter of [choice] but .......... to have basic education in our country.
questions.explanation: Choice (freedom to decide) is opposed to compulsion (being forced).

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

Despite Inyang's claim that he killed the dog .........., the owner insists that he did it [deliberately].
questions.explanation: Deliberately (on purpose) is the opposite of accidentally.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

If our [ancestors] preserved the culture for us, why can't we do the same for our .......... ?
questions.explanation: Ancestors (those who came before) are the opposite of descendants (those who come after).

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

While Mr. Samson is [theoretical] about the upbringing of children, his wife is ..........
questions.explanation: Theoretical is opposed to pragmatic (practical).

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

Whether you [commend] the boys or .......... them, they are determined to do their best.
questions.explanation: Commend (praise) is the opposite of condemn (criticize).

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

The [hope] with which he assumed office contrasts with the .......... with which he is leaving.
questions.explanation: Despair is the absence or opposite of hope.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

The [landing] of a plane is more frightening than its ..........
questions.explanation: A plane's landing is the opposite of its take-off.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

I prefer the [exact] rather than an .......... figure.
questions.explanation: An exact figure is opposed to an approximate one.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) and that will, at the same time, correctly fill the gap in the sentence.

Although the students were [content] with the new welfare arrangement, their representatives were .......... with it.
questions.explanation: Content (satisfied) is the opposite of dissatisfied; 'dissatisfied with' also fits the gap.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The car crashed into a .......... vehicle when the driver lost control.
questions.explanation: Stationary means not moving; stationery means writing materials.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

I told you before the match started that my team would .......... yours.
questions.explanation: One team beats another team; 'win' takes a match or trophy as object.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The Literature teacher instructed us to memorize the first and second .......... of the poem.
questions.explanation: A poem is divided into stanzas.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Gambo was arrested while .......... his late brother as a military officer.
questions.explanation: To impersonate is to pretend to be someone else, usually to deceive, which is an offence.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

He said he would not sell the piece of land because it was the only thing he .......... from his late father.
questions.explanation: Property received from a deceased parent is inherited.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Some church members came to .......... with me on the death of my father.
questions.explanation: One commiserates with someone; 'console' takes a direct object (console me).

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

On that .......... day, nearly five hundred people died in a pipeline explosion.
questions.explanation: A fateful day is one marked by momentous, usually disastrous, events.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

He came to the .......... only two years ago when he won a gold medal.
questions.explanation: To come into the limelight is to become the focus of public attention.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The Road Safety officials will soon be .......... by the government to carry guns.
questions.explanation: To be authorized to do something is to be given official permission.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The man was honoured for fighting .......... in the war.
questions.explanation: Gallantly (bravely) explains why he was honoured.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

Our house is the last but one on that street. This means that our house is
questions.explanation: 'The last but one' is the one just before the last.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

George said he would not attend the meeting because he smelt a rat. This means that he
options: was disturbed by the smell of a rat.
questions.explanation: To smell a rat is to suspect that something is wrong.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

My brother, who lives in Ghana, is a footballer. This means that
options: only one of my brothers lives in Ghana and he is a footballer.
all my brothers are footballers and one lives in Ghana.
my only brother is a footballer and he lives in Ghana.
all my brothers live in Ghana but only one is a footballer.
questions.explanation: The commas mark a non-defining relative clause, so the speaker has only one brother; the clause merely adds information about him.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

The teacher described Edward's account of the incident as a tall story. This means that
options: the teacher could not understand the story.
the teacher found Edward's story unbelievable.
questions.explanation: A tall story is one that is difficult to believe.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

For the past four years, I have been working hard just to keep the wolf from the door. This means that
options: I have not been strong enough to attack the wolf.
I have been able to provide only the basic needs.
I have been working harder than before.
my job has been to prevent the wolf from entering the house.
questions.explanation: To keep the wolf from the door is to earn just enough to avoid hunger and want.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

Ekpong knew there was little food for him at home. This means that
options: Ekpong was sure of some food.
Ekpong was not sure of any food.
Ekpong had hidden some food before going out.
Ekpong's share of the food would not be given to him.
questions.explanation: 'Little' (without 'a') means hardly any, so he could not count on any food; 'a little' would mean some.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

The judge said that he could not but sentence the criminal to death. This means that
options: the judge found it difficult to sentence him to death.
the judge lacked the power to sentence him to death.
it was possible to set the criminal free.
questions.explanation: 'Could not but' means had no choice except to, so the sentence was inevitable.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

The captive shouted several times for help but he knew it was a forlorn hope. This means that he
options: was certain that help would come.
had lost hope of any help coming.
hoped that somebody would hear him.
had lost hope in the captors.
questions.explanation: A forlorn hope is one with almost no chance of success.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

The explanation he gave for the customer's action was a shot in the dark. This means that
options: he only guessed why the customer acted that way.
he knew that the customer liked shooting in the dark.
the customer had told him why he acted that way.
the customer apologized to him in the dark.
questions.explanation: A shot in the dark is a guess.

questions.stem:
Choose the interpretation that you consider most appropriate for the sentence.

Akande stopped short of arresting the man who stole his shoes. This means that Akande
options: arrested him for a while but released him.
thought he was too dangerous to be arrested.
had no option but to arrest him.
was about to arrest him but changed his mind.
questions.explanation: To stop short of doing something is to come close to it but not do it.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

His attempts to claim the child proved [futile].
questions.explanation: Futile attempts are useless and unsuccessful, i.e. abortive.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

These days, most businessmen are very [crafty].
questions.explanation: Crafty means cunning.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

This type of music is [inappropriate] for such a solemn ceremony.
questions.explanation: Inappropriate means unsuitable.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

The clash between the two communities was a great [calamity].
questions.explanation: A calamity is a disaster.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

The negotiations ended [amicably] to the surprise of the warring factions.
questions.explanation: Amicably means in a friendly, harmonious way.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

One needs [perseverance] to succeed in this job.
questions.explanation: Perseverance means persistence in spite of difficulty.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

We did not like him because he was [headstrong].
questions.explanation: Headstrong means stubborn, self-willed.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

The matron [reprimanded] Stella for bullying the new girl.
questions.explanation: To reprimand is to rebuke formally.

questions.topic: Lexis: General Vocabulary in Fields of Human Activity
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that is nearest in meaning to the underlined word (shown in [brackets]) as it is used in the sentence.

His mission was to [enlighten] his people about the proposed project.
questions.explanation: To enlighten is to educate or inform.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The Council of Elders .......... advised youths to desist from telling lies.
questions.explanation: 'The Council' acting as one body takes a singular verb: has advised.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Their ideas are similar, aren't they? Yes, ..........
questions.explanation: A short positive answer repeats the subject and auxiliary: Yes, they are.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

She danced .......... gracefully that the Guest of Honour promised her a special gift.
questions.explanation: The 'so ... that' construction expresses result.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

My father insisted that we should be civil, .......... ?
questions.explanation: The tag agrees with the main clause 'My father insisted' (positive, past): didn't he?

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The team was to leave Lagos .......... Accra at 4.15 a.m. on Tuesday.
questions.explanation: One leaves a place for a destination.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Whenever we .......... our names, we stand up to answer.
questions.explanation: The habitual present ('we stand up') calls for the simple present: hear.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

If I were you, I .......... my identity.
questions.explanation: An unreal (second) conditional takes 'would + base verb' in the main clause.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The judge ruled that the three men should be .......... publicly.
questions.explanation: For execution, the past participle of hang is hanged; hung is used for objects.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Their only child has been sentenced .......... fifteen years' imprisonment.
questions.explanation: One is sentenced to a term of imprisonment.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The governor .......... a good reason to resign before he was impeached.
questions.explanation: Sequence of tenses: the past 'was impeached' requires the past 'had'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Tunde is the .......... in our family.
questions.explanation: 'The ... in our family' implies comparison among more than two: superlative cleverest.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

I wanted to know .......... of the three boys will represent the school.
questions.explanation: 'Which of' selects from a limited group.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Had I been his employer, I .......... him.
questions.explanation: A third conditional (Had I been ...) takes 'would have + past participle'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Before she started crying, she .......... two phone calls.
questions.explanation: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect: had received.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The marriage broke .......... after two years.
questions.explanation: A marriage or relationship breaks up.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Shehu claimed that the money was .......... and not his brother's.
questions.explanation: The possessive pronoun 'his' parallels 'his brother's'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Employers are expected to pay salaries as .......... when due.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'as and when due'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The baby became happy when .......... mother returned.
questions.explanation: A baby whose sex is not stated is referred to as 'it', so the possessive is 'its'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Jane accused her husband .......... dishonesty.
questions.explanation: One accuses someone of something.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

This is the boy to .......... many awards were given on the graduation day.
questions.explanation: After a preposition, the objective form 'whom' is used for persons.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The Principal says that it is you who .......... to conduct the assembly next week.
questions.explanation: The relative 'who' takes the person and number of its antecedent 'you': you who are.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Everyone of our students .......... entitled to free medical treatment.
questions.explanation: 'Everyone' is singular and 'entitled' needs 'is'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Many a student .......... examinations due to lack of preparation.
questions.explanation: 'Many a' takes a singular noun and singular verb.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The old woman did not eat for three days because she did not have .......... money for feeding.
questions.explanation: 'Any' is used in negative sentences.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

We were appointed electoral officers .......... October 2009.
questions.explanation: 'In' is used with months and years.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

You had better .......... off the television.
questions.explanation: 'Had better' is followed by the bare infinitive: turn.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The lady promised to take Bisi and .......... abroad for employment.
questions.explanation: The object of 'take' requires the objective pronoun 'me'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

We do not discuss important issues with her because she is ..........
questions.explanation: 'Talkative' is an adjective and is modified by 'very'; it cannot follow 'a' as a noun.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Her friends are afraid to confide .......... her.
questions.explanation: One confides in someone.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Just .......... milk will improve the taste of this tea.
questions.explanation: 'A little' (a small but positive amount) suits an uncountable noun with a positive effect.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

The teacher told Aminata that she would do .......... in English Language if she took her assignments seriously.
questions.explanation: Comparatives are intensified with 'much', not 'very' or 'more'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

Our tour of the tower came to an end all .......... soon.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is 'all too soon'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

It is important for one to identify with .......... own culture.
questions.explanation: The pronoun must match the antecedent 'one': one's own.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words that best completes the sentence.

You can't expect someone who is always running her friends .......... to be popular.
questions.explanation: To run someone down is to criticize them disparagingly.
